transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well… I hope this is the right place to bring it up. It’s probably going to sound a little complicated, and I don’t want to make it seem bigger than it is, but for months I’ve been noticing this pattern.

My sister’s appointments get moved around, bills come in wrong, people say they’ll call me back and then they “forget.” Everyone keeps telling me these are just mistakes, but it doesn’t feel that way to me. It feels like information is being kept from me, like I’m being pushed out of decisions I should be part of. I just… I need someone to take it seriously, I guess.
How long exactly have you been feeling that people are intentionally keeping information from you or pushing you out of decisions—days, weeks, or longer?

It’s been longer than weeks… I’d say about eleven months, more or less. It really started when my sister’s health suddenly got worse and I had to start coordinating her care. I mean, I’m not trying to make it sound dramatic, but that’s when I started feeling like I wasn’t being told things or included the way I should be.
Have you experienced hearing voices, or seeing or sensing things that others around you don't seem to notice?

No… I don’t think so. I mean, not voices or seeing things, if that’s what you mean. I haven’t had anything like that. It’s more just… noticing how things are handled, and what people say or don’t say. But no, nothing that other people couldn’t see or hear, I don’t believe.

Do you find yourself feeling this same kind of suspicion or distrust in other areas of your life—like with friends, coworkers, or people in general—or is it really just centered on this situation with your sister's care?

It’s… mostly centered on my sister’s care, I think. I don’t want to sound like I’m suspicious of everybody, because I’m not trying to be difficult.

But with this situation, it’s been the same thing over and over for months—appointments getting moved, bills being wrong, people saying they’ll call and then not doing it. And everyone says, “Oh, it’s just a mistake,” but it doesn’t feel like just mistakes to me. It feels like they know more than they’re telling me, and like they’re trying to keep me out of decisions I should be part of.

Before your sister's health declined about eleven months ago, would you say you generally trusted people and their intentions, or has this kind of suspicion and difficulty trusting others been part of how you've felt since you were younger?

I think before all this, I was generally pretty trusting. I mean, I wasn’t naïve, but I didn’t go around assuming people were keeping things from me. This really started about eleven months ago, when my sister’s health suddenly got worse and I had to start helping coordinate her care. Since then it’s been… harder for me to feel like I’m being told everything. Is that what you mean?

Has this experience affected your ability to function in other areas of your life—like your job, your relationships, or taking care of yourself—or has it stayed pretty contained to dealing with your sister's care situation?

I think it’s stayed pretty contained, mostly. I mean, I’m still going to work, I’m keeping up with my bills, my house isn’t falling apart or anything like that. I take care of what I need to take care of.

I know some people might say I’m too focused on what’s happening with my sister’s appointments and trying to get straight answers, and maybe I do spend a lot of energy on it. But I’m not acting strangely in other parts of my life, at least I don’t think so. I’m functioning, you know?

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a fixed, non-bizarre delusional belief (that family/medical staff are deliberately withholding information and excluding her from her sister's care decisions) persisting for approximately 11 months. There are no hallucinations, no other positive psychotic symptoms (disorganized speech, negative symptoms), and no evidence of a mood episode preceding or accompanying the delusion. The delusion is circumscribed to the specific situation involving her sister's care, and overall functioning (work, self-care, finances) remains intact, arguing against schizophrenia (which requires broader functional decline and/or other psychotic symptoms) and against a mood disorder with psychotic features. The acute onset in adulthood in the context of a specific stressor (sister's illness), without a longstanding pervasive pattern of distrust across all relationships since a young age, argues against paranoid personality disorder. This clinical picture—an isolated, persistent, non-bizarre persecutory delusion lasting more than one month with preserved functioning outside the delusional theme—meets criteria for Delusional Disorder (F22).
